title: Impact of ROTEM® Use in Oncology Patients Undergoing Cancer Surgery: A Retrospective Historical Cohort Study
content: Background/Objectives: Major oncologic surgery is frequently associated with substantial blood loss and perioperative coagulopathy. Conventional coagulation tests provide limited and delayed assessment during active bleeding, whereas rotational thromboelastometry (ROTEM) enables real-time evaluation of clot formation. This study evaluated the transfusion and clinical impact of ROTEM guided hemostatic management in major oncologic surgery. Methods: This retrospective historical cohort study included 137 adults undergoing elective oncologic surgery at a specialized cancer center between January 2020 and December 2023. Patients with intraoperative bleeding received either conventional management (n = 90) or ROTEM guided management (n = 47). Demographic and clinical characteristics, surgical risk, estimated blood loss, transfusion requirements, vasoactive drug use, and hospital length of stay were compared. A predefined subgroup of 79 patients undergoing complex oncologic procedures was also analyzed. Results: Baseline characteristics were comparable between groups. Overall, 87.6% of procedures were high risk, and 73.7% of patients had blood loss >1000 mL. Transfusion requirements did not differ significantly in the overall cohort. In complex oncologic surgery, ROTEM guided management was associated with fewer patients receiving fresh frozen plasma than conventional management (24.2% vs. 54.3%, p = 0.011). Red blood cell transfusion was numerically lower with ROTEM, while vasoactive drug use and hospital length of stay did not differ significantly. Conclusions: ROTEM guided management was associated with reduced fresh frozen plasma exposure in complex oncologic surgery, supporting a more targeted transfusion strategy. Prospective studies are needed to confirm its effects on clinical outcomes.
